subject: chemistry
title: Hydrocarbons and fuels
summary: Alkanes and alkenes, how to name them, how crude oil is separated by fractional distillation, and what happens when hydrocarbon fuels burn.
body:
Petrol, diesel, the LPG in a barbecue bottle and the natural gas in a kitchen stove are all made mostly of hydrocarbons. These compounds supply much of the world's energy and are also the raw materials for plastics, medicines and many other products. Learning how they are named, separated and burned is your first step into **organic chemistry**, the chemistry of carbon compounds, which is a large part of VCE.

## Think of it like this

### A homologous series is like a Lego train that grows one carriage at a time

Imagine building trains from identical Lego carriages, where each new train is one carriage longer than the last. In a **homologous series** each member is one CH₂ unit longer than the one before: methane, ethane, propane, butane and so on. The **prefix** (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-) tells you how many carbon "carriages" are in the chain, and the **suffix** (-ane or -ene) tells you which family of train it is. Because every train is built the same way, they all follow the same rule – for **alkanes**, the **general formula** CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* Lego carriages are all the same, but the carbons at the ends of a chain carry three hydrogens (CH₃) while the middle ones carry two (CH₂), and real chains can also branch.

### Fractional distillation is like a crowded tram emptying stop by stop

Picture a tram full of passengers, where each passenger gets off at the stop that matches their "boiling point". The hot vapour of **crude oil** enters the bottom of the **fractionating column** and rises, cooling as it goes. Big, heavy hydrocarbons with high boiling points "get off" first, condensing near the hot bottom as fuel oil and bitumen. Small molecules with low boiling points stay on all the way to the cool top, coming off as refinery gases and petrol. Each stop collects a **fraction** of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* passengers get off one by one at an exact stop, but each fraction is a mixture of many hydrocarbons, and chain lengths overlap between fractions.

### Complete versus incomplete combustion is like a barbecue with or without enough air

When a gas barbecue has plenty of air, the flame burns clean and blue – that is **complete combustion**, where the hydrocarbon reacts fully with oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water and releases the most energy. Block the air vents and you get a yellow, sooty flame: **incomplete combustion**, with not enough oxygen to turn all the carbon into CO₂. Instead you get soot (carbon) and the poisonous gas carbon monoxide, and less energy is released. It's like trying to cook a full meal with half the ingredients – you get something, but not the full result.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* the colour of a flame is a useful clue but not a reliable test – carbon monoxide has no colour or smell, so you can't safely judge it by looking.

### In real life

The LPG bottle on a barbecue holds propane and butane from the refinery-gas fraction, and the petrol and diesel at the servo come from the middle of the column. Gas heaters must be well ventilated and serviced because incomplete combustion can produce carbon monoxide, which is why carbon monoxide alarms are used in some homes.

## Key ideas

### What is a hydrocarbon?

A **hydrocarbon** is a compound made of hydrogen and carbon atoms *only*. Carbon is special because each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds and can bond to other carbon atoms, making chains of almost any length. Hydrogen forms one bond.

### Alkanes

**Alkanes** are hydrocarbons in which all the carbon–carbon bonds are single bonds. Because every carbon has the greatest possible number of hydrogen atoms attached, alkanes are described as **saturated**.

All alkanes fit the **general formula** CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, where n is the number of carbon atoms. A group of compounds with the same general formula and similar chemical properties, where each member differs from the next by CH₂, is called a **homologous series**.

### Alkenes

**Alkenes** are hydrocarbons that contain one carbon–carbon double bond (C=C). Because they have fewer hydrogen atoms than the matching alkane, they are **unsaturated**. Alkenes with one double bond have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ. The smallest alkene has two carbons, because a double bond needs two carbon atoms.

The double bond makes alkenes more **reactive** than alkanes. Other atoms can add across the double bond. A simple test uses bromine water: an alkene quickly turns orange-brown bromine water colourless, while an alkane does not (at least not quickly, in the dark).

### Naming alkanes and alkenes

Names have two parts. The **prefix** tells you the number of carbon atoms in the chain; the **suffix** tells you the family: **-ane** for alkanes and **-ene** for alkenes.

| Carbons | Prefix | Alkane | Formula | Alkene | Formula |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | meth- | methane | CH₄ | — | — |
| 2 | eth- | ethane | C₂H₆ | ethene | C₂H₄ |
| 3 | prop- | propane | C₃H₈ | propene | C₃H₆ |
| 4 | but- | butane | C₄H₁₀ | butene | C₄H₈ |
| 5 | pent- | pentane | C₅H₁₂ | pentene | C₅H₁₀ |
| 6 | hex- | hexane | C₆H₁₄ | hexene | C₆H₁₂ |

For alkenes with four or more carbons, the double bond can be in different places, so a number shows where it starts. Count from the end nearer the double bond: CH₂=CH–CH₂–CH₃ is **but-1-ene**, and CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃ is **but-2-ene**.

### Structural formulas

A **molecular formula** such as C₃H₈ shows only the number of each atom. A **structural formula** shows how the atoms are joined. Propane can be written in condensed form as CH₃–CH₂–CH₃ and propene as CH₂=CH–CH₃. Always check every carbon has exactly four bonds (a double bond counts as two).

### Physical properties

As the chain gets longer, the molecules have stronger forces of attraction between them (called **dispersion forces**). So:

- **boiling point increases**: methane to butane are gases at room temperature, pentane to about C₁₆ are liquids, and longer chains are waxy solids
- **viscosity increases**: longer-chain liquids are thicker and flow less easily
- **flammability decreases**: short chains catch fire more easily

Hydrocarbons do not dissolve in water.

### Crude oil and fractional distillation

**Crude oil** (petroleum) is a fossil fuel formed over millions of years from the remains of tiny sea organisms buried under heat and pressure. It is a mixture of many hydrocarbons, mostly alkanes, with different chain lengths. To be useful it must be separated.

**Fractional distillation** separates the mixture into **fractions**: groups of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points.

1. Crude oil is heated until most of it becomes vapour.
2. The vapour enters the bottom of a tall **fractionating column**, which is hot at the bottom and cooler towards the top.
3. As the vapour rises, it cools. Each hydrocarbon condenses back to a liquid when it reaches a level cooler than its boiling point, and is collected there.
4. Small molecules with low boiling points rise to the top (for example refinery gases and petrol). Large molecules with high boiling points condense near the bottom (for example lubricating oil and bitumen for roads).

| Fraction (top to bottom) | Approximate chain length | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Refinery gases | C₁–C₄ | LPG, bottled gas |
| Petrol (gasoline) | C₅–C₁₀ | car fuel |
| Kerosene | C₁₀–C₁₆ | jet fuel |
| Diesel | C₁₄–C₂₀ | trucks, trains |
| Fuel oil and lubricating oil | C₂₀–C₄₀ | ships, machine oil |
| Bitumen | more than C₄₀ | roads, roofing |

Chain lengths overlap slightly between fractions and vary between refineries.

### Combustion of fuels

A **fuel** is a substance that releases useful energy when it burns. **Combustion** is a reaction with oxygen that releases heat; it is **exothermic**.

With plenty of oxygen, hydrocarbons undergo **complete combustion**, producing carbon dioxide and water:

`CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g)`

With limited oxygen, **incomplete combustion** occurs, producing carbon monoxide (CO), a poisonous gas with no colour or smell, and/or soot (carbon, C), as well as water. Less energy is released. This is why gas heaters need good ventilation and regular servicing.

`2CH₄(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO(g) + 4H₂O(g)`

Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas linked to climate change. Impurities such as sulfur produce sulfur dioxide, which contributes to acid rain. Crude oil is also **non-renewable**: it forms far more slowly than we use it.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Formula and name

Write the molecular formula of the alkane with 5 carbons, and name it.

- General formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 5: H = 2 × 5 + 2 = 12
- Formula: C₅H₁₂; prefix pent- plus -ane gives **pentane**

### Example 2: Balancing a combustion equation

Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of propane, C₃H₈.

- Step 1: C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
- Step 2: Balance C: 3 CO₂
- Step 3: Balance H: 8 H gives 4 H₂O
- Step 4: Count O on the right: 3 × 2 + 4 × 1 = 10, so 5 O₂

`C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(g)`

## Common mistakes

- Thinking "methene" exists. An alkene needs at least two carbons.
- Mixing up saturated (alkane, single bonds only) and unsaturated (alkene, contains C=C).
- Thinking the biggest molecules come out at the top of the fractionating column. Small, low-boiling molecules rise highest.
- Forgetting that incomplete combustion makes carbon monoxide and soot, not just less carbon dioxide.
- Balancing oxygen first in combustion equations. Balance C, then H, then O last.

## Exam tips

- Learn the prefixes meth- to hex- by heart; naming questions are quick marks.
- Explain trends in boiling point by referring to chain length and the strength of forces between molecules.
- For fractional distillation, mention both "different boiling points" and "temperature gradient in the column".
- Always include states in combustion equations.

## Tips to remember

- **"Monkeys Eat Peanut Butter"** – meth (1), eth (2), prop (3), but (4) carbons. After that, pent (5) and hex (6) match pentagon and hexagon.
- **-ane = all single bonds (saturated); -ene = an extra bond, one C=C (unsaturated).** There is no "methene": a double bond needs two carbons.
- **Formula shortcuts:** for an alkane, double the carbons and add two (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂). For an alkene, just double them (CₙH₂ₙ). For example, pentane is C₅H₁₂.
- **Fractional distillation, a made-up rhyme: "Little ones fly high, big ones stay low."** Small, low-boiling molecules (gases, petrol) come out at the top. Big ones (bitumen) come out at the bottom.
- **Balance combustion equations in "C-H-O" order:** carbon first, then hydrogen, then oxygen last.
- **Not enough oxygen means danger.** Incomplete combustion makes carbon monoxide (poisonous, with no colour or smell) and soot. That is why gas heaters need ventilation.

## Key terms

- **Hydrocarbon** — a compound containing only carbon and hydrogen.
- **Alkane** — a saturated hydrocarbon with only single C–C bonds; CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
- **Alkene** — an unsaturated hydrocarbon with one C=C double bond; CₙH₂ₙ.
- **Homologous series** — a family of compounds with the same general formula, each differing by CH₂.
- **Fraction** — a group of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points separated from crude oil.
- **Fractional distillation** — separating a mixture of liquids by their different boiling points.
- **Complete combustion** — burning in plenty of oxygen to give CO₂ and H₂O.
- **Incomplete combustion** — burning in limited oxygen to give CO and/or C, and H₂O.

## Summary

- Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen.
- Alkanes have single bonds (saturated); alkenes have a C=C double bond (unsaturated) and are more reactive.
- Names use a prefix for the carbon count and -ane or -ene for the family.
- Crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation, using differences in boiling point.
- Complete combustion gives CO₂ and H₂O; incomplete combustion also gives CO or soot.

questions.explanation: C₄H₈ fits the alkene formula CₙH₂ₙ (n = 4, 2n = 8), so it is butene. C₃H₈, C₅H₁₂ and C₂H₆ all fit CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and are alkanes; C₂H₆ is tempting because it starts with eth-, like ethene, but ethene is C₂H₄.

questions.prompt: What is the name of CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃?
questions.explanation: There are five carbons in a chain joined only by single bonds, so it is pentane. Pentene is tempting but would need a C=C double bond. Butane has only four carbons.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly explains why alkenes decolourise bromine water quickly but alkanes do not?

options.A: Alkenes have a C=C double bond that other atoms can add across
options.B: Alkenes contain more hydrogen atoms than alkanes
options.C: Alkanes do not contain carbon–carbon bonds

questions.explanation: The double bond in an alkene makes it reactive: bromine adds across it, removing the colour. Option B is the reverse of the truth; alkenes have fewer hydrogens than the matching alkane. Alkanes are saturated, not unsaturated.

questions.prompt: In a fractionating column, why do petrol fractions collect higher up than diesel fractions?

options.A: Petrol molecules are heavier and are pushed up by the vapour
options.B: Petrol molecules are shorter, have lower boiling points and stay as vapour until the cooler top of the column
options.C: Petrol is more viscous than diesel
options.D: The top of the column is hotter than the bottom

questions.explanation: Shorter chains have weaker forces between molecules and lower boiling points, so they rise further before condensing in the cooler upper part of the column. Option D is tempting but reversed: the column is hottest at the bottom.

questions.prompt: As the number of carbon atoms in an alkane chain increases, which change occurs?
questions.explanation: Longer chains have stronger dispersion forces between molecules, so they flow less easily (higher viscosity) and have higher boiling points. Flammability actually decreases with chain length, and hydrocarbons stay insoluble in water.

questions.prompt: Which products form during incomplete combustion of a hydrocarbon?

options.A: Carbon monoxide and/or carbon, and water

questions.explanation: With limited oxygen, carbon is not fully oxidised, so carbon monoxide and/or soot form, along with water. Option B describes complete combustion, the most common confusion.

questions.prompt: In the balanced equation for the complete combustion of butane, 2C₄H₁₀(g) + xO₂(g) → 8CO₂(g) + 10H₂O(g), what is x?
questions.explanation: Oxygen atoms on the right: 8 × 2 + 10 × 1 = 26, so x = 26 ÷ 2 = 13 O₂. 26 is tempting but is the number of oxygen atoms, not O₂ molecules.

questions.prompt: What is the molecular formula of hexene?
questions.explanation: Hex- means 6 carbons and -ene means an alkene, CₙH₂ₙ, so C₆H₁₂. C₆H₁₄ is hexane, the alkane. C₅H₁₀ is pentene.
